title: The roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8–9)
hookLine: be sober and watch: read every Tuesday at night prayer
tomorrow: a thousand years as a day

cards: It's late on a Tuesday. In a monastery chapel, a convent, a hospital break room, a bedroom with a phone propped on the pillow, people are praying the last prayer of the Church's day, called Compline, or Night Prayer.
The lights are low. The psalm is done. And the short reading for Tuesday night is two verses from the end of First Peter.
In the older form of the prayer, those same verses opened Compline every night, right before the lights go out.

teach.b: Here they are in the Douay-Rheims: "Be sober and watch: because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour." Two commands first.
Be sober: the Greek means clear-headed, not drunk, not foggy. And watch: stay awake, keep alert. That second word has a history for Peter.

teach.h: WATCH: PETER SLEPT IN THE GARDEN.
teach.b: On the night before Jesus died, in the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus asked Peter to watch with him for one hour. Peter fell asleep, more than once. Now the same man, years later, tells the whole Church: stay awake.
Then the picture: a lion, prowling, roaring, looking for someone to swallow. A prowler in the dark is a night fear, which is one reason the verse sits well at bedtime.

The Church teaches that the devil is real, a fallen creature, but a creature: not God's equal, with limits on what he can do. So Peter doesn't say run, or panic. He says, "Whom resist ye, strong in faith."
Stand your ground. And he adds something easy to miss: your brothers and sisters all over the world are going through the same sufferings.

teach.h: THE LION LOOKS FOR THE ONE ALONE.
teach.b: In the picture, the lion looks for the one who's alone.
The answer is a clear head, open eyes, and a whole flock.
Night Prayer is shaped for this. It begins with a short look back over the day, and it ends by entrusting the night to God.

how: In the Liturgy of the Hours, Night Prayer (Compline) begins with an examination of conscience and, on Tuesdays, has 1 Peter 5:8–9 as its short reading; priests, religious and some lay Catholics pray it before sleep.

games.q: you're Peter in the garden of Gethsemane. Jesus asks you to stay awake and watch with him for one hour. it's late, and you're exhausted. what happens?
o: you stay awake and pray the whole hour.
you go back to the city for help.
games.why: Peter falls asleep, more than once. years later the same man writes to the whole Church: be sober and watch.

practice: Sit up a little, as if keeping watch, and walk back through today, slowly, from now to this morning: where you were clear-headed, where you drifted, scrolled or snapped.
Don't judge it, just see it, the way a watchman sees the walls, and notice one moment you'd like to handle differently tomorrow.
If you pray, hand the night to God, or pray a line from Compline if you know one; if not, close the day with your eyes open to it.

wordCard.voice: Compline, the Church's last prayer of the day. Where First Peter's warning about the roaring lion is read, right before the lights go out. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin (Vulgate): be sober, and watch: the words that opened Compline in the older Roman breviary.

carryVoice: Your line: be sober, watch. Clear-headed, awake, and never the one left alone. Good night.
